function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

I’m not able to run commands or push to a remote repository from here, but I can walk you through the exact steps you’d need to take on your own machine (or in a CI job) to accomplish everything you listed.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
# SSH clone – make sure you have the key added to your agent
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

If you prefer HTTPS:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & generate artefacts

### 2.1 Inspect the repo

Run a quick scan to see what the repo contains:

```bash
# List files
tree -L 2

# Check package.json
cat package.json
```

Typical output might look like:

```
nodejs-welcome/
├── src/
│   └── index.js
├── package.json
└── README.md
```

From this you’ll know:

- The entry point (`src/index.js` or `index.js`).
- The Node.js version (look in `engines` field of `package.json` or `.nvmrc`).
- Any build steps (e.g., `npm run build`).

### 2.2 Create / update the Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` in the repo root with the following content (adjust the Node version if needed):

```dockerfile
# Use an official Node runtime as a parent image
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set the working directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy package files first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the application
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD ["node", "src/index.js"]
```

> **Tip** – If your app uses a build step (`npm run build`), add `RUN npm run build` before the final `COPY . .`.

### 2.3 Generate Kubernetes YAML

Create a file `k8s/deployment.yaml` (you can keep it in a `k8s/` folder or at the repo root):

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: <YOUR_REGISTRY>/nodejs-welcome:latest   # replace with your image repo
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
  type: ClusterIP
```

> **Note** – Replace `<YOUR_REGISTRY>` with the registry you’ll push to (e.g., `ghcr.io/zelarhq`).

### 2.4 Create a GitHub Actions workflow

Create a file `.github/workflows/docker-build.yml`:

```yaml
name: Build & Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - name: Checkout code
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

    - name: Log in to GitHub Container Registry
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        registry: ghcr.io
        username: ${{ github.actor }}
        password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Build and push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        file: ./Dockerfile
        push: true
        tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

> **Prerequisites** –  
> * The repo must be under a GitHub organization or user that has permissions to push to `ghcr.io`.  
> * The default `GITHUB_TOKEN` has write access to the registry for the repo, so no extra secrets are needed.

---

## 3️⃣ Add the new files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/docker-build.yml
```

If you want to commit all changes (including any modifications you made to existing files):

```bash
git add -u
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

Once pushed, the GitHub Actions workflow will trigger automatically on the `push` event, building the image and pushing it to `ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest`.

---

### Quick checklist

| ✅ | Task |
|---|------|
| ✅ | Clone repo |
| ✅ | Inspect repo structure |
| ✅ | Create Dockerfile (Node 18 Alpine) |
| ✅ | Create Kubernetes deployment & service YAML |
| ✅ | Create GitHub Actions workflow to build & push image |
| ✅ | Add files to Git |
| ✅ | Commit & push |

That’s it! After the workflow completes, you’ll have a Docker image ready in GitHub Container Registry, and you can deploy it to any Kubernetes cluster using the generated YAML.
